new_statements.quote: p. 149: "rhetorical lengthening is a useful diagnostic for stress placement. Many speakers have a difficult time deciding where primary stress falls on words with more that one vowel. The problem is nearly solved by adding rhetorical length to one of the vowels. Speakers will add it with regularity to the vowel that in normal speech is stressed." p. 152: "When stems that contain the sequence ʔV́ lose the stressed vowel to a strong suffix, they replace it with a (unstressed) as in the examples that follow." p. 158, §4.7 Ambivalent stress: "There are many cases of different stress valences that signify different lexical import; but there are also cases of dialectal and idiolectal variation. Here I provide only four examples: nt'iɬps ~ nt'ɬúps. Dirty bottom [...] ta nsílxcən ~ ta nsəlxcín in Indian"

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for okan1243 has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so nothing to agree or conflict with. This paper supplies only indirect, compatible content: a morphologically conditioned system (strong suffixes take stress from the stem), lexically contrastive stress, and reported variation. It is not a placement statement in itself; the placement rule is in the already-downloaded Mattina 1973 grammar held by the project (§2.541 'Stress placement', pp. 25-27), which is outside this task's works list.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The paper never states a placement rule. It presupposes one: stems carry the stress unless a 'strong suffix' takes it (the stem's stressed vowel is then lost and replaced by unstressed a), i.e. stress is governed by the morphological make-up of the word (root vs. stress-attracting suffix), not by syllable position or weight. It adds that stress is lexically distinctive in many word pairs ('different stress valences that signify different lexical import'), that speakers often cannot say where primary stress falls in polysyllables (rhetorical lengthening on the stressed vowel is the diagnostic), and that some words show dialectal and idiolectal stress variation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; only 'primary stress' is mentioned (p. 149).
new_statements.exceptions: §4.7 lists four words with alternating stress (nt'iɬps ~ nt'ɬúps 'dirty bottom'; kən tk'ʷíƛ'pxan ~ kən tk'ʷƛ'pxan 'my shoe came off'; m'áy'aʔɬtsən ~ m'ay'ɬtsín 'I told you'; ta nsílxcən ~ ta nsəlxcín 'in Indian'), attributed to lexical contrast or to dialectal/idiolectal variation. Unstressed word-final vowels may also carry rhetorical length, competing with the stressed-vowel lengthening (p. 149).
new_statements.identity_note: Mattina 2000 describes 'Okanagan' as spoken by his Colville-Okanagan consultants (author affiliations: University of Montana, En'okwin Centre, Colville Language Preservation; speaker initials RA, SL cited); the ambivalent-stress examples in §4.7 are explicitly attributed in part to dialectal and idiolectal variation within Okanagan. No specific dialect (Colville vs. Douglas Lake, etc.) is named for the stress remarks.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: both deciding passages (Mattina 1973 sec. 2.3 p.13 and sec. 2.541 pp.25-27) and both Pattison 1978 passages (sec. 1.6 p.11, sec. 2.4 p.15) are verbatim at the stated places in the copies we hold; Mattina 1973 was re-confirmed in an open ERIC copy (ED087201) saved today, which also cures a copy whose provenance we do not cite provenance of the 9/12 PDF. Deciding source: a 1973 PhD grammar by the language's principal describer, Glottolog's top-ranked and only 'grammar' entry; the classification 'morphological' (lexical-accent system: stress by root class and suffix class, prefixes unstressed, one primary stress per word) is exactly what the source states. Best-available check: Glottolog's one larger competitor, Watkins 1970 (752 pp U Alberta PhD phonology+morphology of the Head of the Lake dialect), was downloaded from archive.org and read (pp.302-314): it sets up three stress classes of stems (A/B/C) a
